1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3.background: A common start of the King's Indian Attack, which Bobby Fischer (mostly in his early career), Mikhail Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov and Tigran Petrosian all employed. Its use at grandmaster level began in the 1950s as an offshoot of the widespread King's Indian Defence, with White adopting Black's set-up with an extra move.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.name: King's Indian Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.background: Relatively uncommon at grandmaster level today, with Bassem Amin its most frequent high-level practitioner, but popular at club level for its repeatable middlegame plans. The trainer Mark Dvoretsky advocated the system and played it himself.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and keeps the c8-bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. The cost is a committed d-pawn, which gives White a clear target for c4 and the plan of building up with d3 and e4. The game tends to be closed and strategic, with White setting the pace.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6.name: King's Indian Attack: Symmetrical Defence
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's kingside fianchetto: the bishop will watch the long diagonal and the king can castle early, while the centre stays open for later. If White takes space with c4 and d4, the game becomes a King's Indian or a Grünfeld with White's bishop on g2. The cost is a slower claim on the centre than ...d5 makes at once.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Controls d4, so White cannot easily build a broad centre, and keeps the d-pawn flexible. Black can head for a symmetrical set-up or for a Reversed King's Indian, taking White's usual role. The c-pawn occupies no central square yet, so both sides keep their options.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 with a solid set-up. The cost is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn unless Black finds a way out, such as a queenside fianchetto; White's slow build-up with d3 and e4 aims at exactly that. White can also take space with c4 and d4, with the g2-bishop pressing on the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.name: King's Indian Attack: Spassky Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.background: Sometimes called the Spassky Variation after Boris Spassky's use of ...b5 against Tigran Petrosian in the 1966 World Championship match, although that game, the decisive 22nd, began 1.d4 b5. The line is fully respectable and has been played successfully by grandmasters including former world champions Mikhail Tal, Anatoly Karpov and Magnus Carlsen.
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...Bb7 to contest the long diagonal. Unlike ...b6, it discourages c4, since the pawn on b5 could take there. The price is a pawn that can become a target for White's a-pawn and knight and a loosened queenside.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to oppose the bishop on g2 on the long diagonal. The set-up is sound, but unlike ...b5 it does not discourage c4, so White can take space in the centre or play quietly.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight towards d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5, which it would support. It blocks the c-pawn, ruling out ...c5 for now, and White can take the centre with d4. The move is sound but less flexible than set-ups that keep the c-pawn free.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn chain, with the c8-bishop free to go to f5 or g4 once the d-pawn advances. The move does nothing for the centre yet, so White can take the centre first. Sound, but ...d5 at once reaches the same set-ups and keeps the c-pawn free for ...c5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and a compact set-up behind it. It opens the c8-bishop but concedes central space, so White can build a broad centre. Sound, though passive.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 a6.strategy: A slow move that prepares ...b5, which Black could play at once. Nothing is lost, since White has no way to punish it, but Black spends a tempo on an edge pawn while White builds the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and controls b4, but does nothing for development or the centre. The position stays sound, yet Black has spent a tempo on an edge pawn and White can build up undisturbed.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the edge, where it eyes b4 and c5 but has little influence on the centre. White gains time to build there.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Rg8.strategy: Gives up kingside castling for good, since the h8-rook has moved, and the rook does nothing on g8. Black has lost a tempo and White builds a full centre unopposed, which gives away real ground.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ng8.strategy: Undoes the first move. Black has spent two tempi to return to the start while White has developed the knight and prepared the fianchetto, with a free hand in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 h6.strategy: A prophylactic pawn move that covers g5, though nothing threatens it yet. It spends a tempo that development needs, but White cannot punish it, so Black is only slow while White builds the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Heads for ...h4 to challenge the g3-pawn, but loosens the kingside before Black has developed and does nothing for the centre. White can simply build there, so the move is sound but second-rate.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ng4.strategy: The knight eyes f2 and h2 from g4, but 3.h3 chases it at once, and 3...Ne5 then loses it to Nxe5. After the retreat to f6 or h6 Black has lost two tempi and White has played h3 for free.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes g3 and f4 but contests no central square. White can build the centre, or drive it away at once with 3.g4, gaining kingside space with tempo.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but 3.c4 attacks it at once and it must retreat, for example to b6. White gains time for a broad centre, while Black has spent three moves on one knight.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 Ne4.strategy: Eyes f2 and g3, but 3.d3 attacks the knight at once and it must retreat to f6, d6 or c5, losing time while White gains d3 for free. Capturing on g3 only gives a knight for a pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: the knight on f6 does not guard g5, so 3.Nxg5 simply wins it, and Black's kingside is left loose.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Hangs the e-pawn: nothing defends e5, so 3.Nxe5 simply wins it. After 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 Black's queen and c8-bishop have open lines, but Black is a clean pawn down.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop to its post on the long diagonal and prepares castling. White has a flexible set-up: the centre can be taken with the e-pawn or with the c-pawn, and Black must decide how to meet a system rather than a particular move.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.d4.strategy: Takes a broad pawn centre at once, with the king's bishop to follow on the long diagonal. White gives up the flexible, slow build-up for a more direct fight over the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 straight away, with the king's bishop to join the fight for the centre from g2. It asks Black whether to hold the centre or take on c4 and give the pawn back later; White accepts a more open, queenside-oriented game than a quiet build-up.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Supports the d5 pawn while leaving the queen's bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. A solid, compact set-up that avoids the cramped bishop that the other natural defence brings.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6.name: King's Indian Attack, with e6
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the way for the king's bishop. It is solid, but the queen's bishop is shut in behind the e6 and d5 pawns, so Black must find a plan to bring it into play while White builds up patiently.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre from the flank and keeps the position fluid: Black gains queenside space and can later build a compact pawn centre of its own, with the king's bishop and the knights still free to choose their squares.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles before committing the centre. White's set-up is complete and the choice of central plan stays open, which is the strength of the system: Black has to guess which pawn break is coming.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.d3.strategy: The classic set-up of the system: White builds the e4 centre from behind with the d-pawn, instead of striking at d5. It is slow and flexible, aiming for a central pawn push and a kingside attack while Black's queen's bishop stays shut in.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.c4.strategy: Puts the c-pawn against d5 before castling and aims at a long-term pull on the centre and the queenside. White trades the quiet central build-up for a more direct fight over d5.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7.name: King's Indian Attack, with e6
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7.strategy: Brings the king's bishop out and prepares to castle, keeping the position compact and safe. Black is solid but still waiting: White has finished development and can pick the plan that suits it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O c5.strategy: The thematic reply to the fianchetto system: Black strikes at the centre with a flank pawn and keeps the choice of set-up open. Black gets active queenside play and takes control of d4, so White has to decide how to meet the challenge.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Nbd7.strategy: Develops the queen's knight behind the centre pawns and prepares to meet White's central plans with a pawn break of Black's own. It is a solid and flexible set-up, but it gives White time to choose its plan while Black's queen's bishop is still shut in.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7 5.c.strategy: Gives up the slower plan with the e-pawn and presses on the d5 pawn directly. The position takes on the character of a closed game in which White's pieces and the c-pawn together test Black's centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 d5 3.Bg2 e6 4.O-O Be7 5.d.strategy: The main set-up of the system: White prepares the e4 centre from behind and keeps the knights flexible. The plan is slow but reliable, a central pawn push to cramp Black followed by pressure on the kingside, with a solid pawn structure that gives Black no target.
Takes the centre with a pawn and fixes a classical structure. White gives up the flexibility of the slow build-up for a more open game.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2.strategy: The natural completion of the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at the centre and the queenside, and White can castle next. It commits to a flexible, patient set-up in which White builds behind the pawns and chooses the central plan later.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares a second fianchetto, with a bishop on b2 as well, so that both bishops eye the centre from a distance. The pawn on b3 weakens nothing urgent, but White gives up some flexibility: the set-up is aimed at the long diagonals rather than at the centre pawns.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b4.name: King's Indian Attack: Smyslov Variation
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space at once and prepares the bishop for b2, behind the pawn on the long diagonal. The cost is that the b-pawn stands undefended and can be challenged by Black's queenside pawns, while the kingside pieces are still at home: ambitious, but second-rate.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7.strategy: Black completes the fianchetto in the same way: the bishop presses on the centre from the long diagonal and the king is ready to castle behind the g6 pawn. A solid, symmetrical answer that makes the second white fianchetto no threat.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and controls e4 and c4. The pawn then has to be supported by pieces and will be challenged by a pawn of White's, so the game becomes a direct fight for the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 c5.strategy: Takes queenside space and the d4 square before White's bishop reaches the long diagonal, a more combative set-up than simply mirroring White. The price is a pawn that can become a target once White prepares to attack it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2.strategy: Finishes the queenside fianchetto: the bishop eyes the knight on f6 and the e5 square, and with the king's bishop to come White controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. The game stays quiet and manoeuvring, with the pawn breaks still to be chosen.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the kingside bishop first and leaves the other bishop for the next move. The same double fianchetto arises, so this is a question of move order rather than of plan: White keeps the choice of the centre pawn structure open.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.c4.strategy: Takes queenside space and controls d5 before the bishops are out, so Black's central break is held back. The cost is time and commitment: the c-pawn moves before the king is safe and the other bishop is still undeveloped.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O.strategy: Black tucks the king away behind the fianchetto pawns and lets White show the plan. Nothing is conceded in the centre, and the rook on f8 gets ready to support a later pawn advance there.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 d5.strategy: Claims central space at once, controlling e4 and c4. Black commits the structure early and must keep the pawn supported against a c-pawn break.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 d6.strategy: Holds e5, the square the bishop on b2 and the knight on f3 both aim at, and frees the queen's bishop. Black keeps the structure flexible and gives White nothing to attack, at the price of leaving the centre to White for now.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.strategy: Completes the double fianchetto: both bishops now bear on long diagonals, and castling is White's next step. The set-up asks Black to find a plan, since White has not yet committed a single central pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.c.strategy: Takes queenside space and the d5 square, so Black's central break becomes harder, and leaves the bishops to work on the long diagonals. The cost is that White's king is still uncastled and the c-pawn has left the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.d.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn at last, which turns the game into a queen's-pawn structure with fianchettoed bishops. White gains space, but the bishop on b2 now looks at its own pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.strategy: A solid reply: the pawn on d6 holds the e5 square and frees the c8-bishop, while Black keeps every plan open for the middlegame. It is less direct than a claim on the centre, but it leaves nothing to attack.

The principled reply: Black takes the centre while White has no central pawn, and the pawn controls e4 and c4. White's pieces must now work against a solid centre. The cost is a committed structure that Black has to keep supported.

Challenges the centre from the flank, taking control of d4 and gaining queenside space. It contests d4 on the diagonal of the bishop on b2 and keeps the d-pawn flexible, but the c-pawn can become a target once White prepares to attack it.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.name: Zukertort Opening: Double Fianchetto Attack
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.b3 Bg7 4.Bb2 O-O 5.B.strategy: Finishes the development of the set-up and safeguards the king. From here the game is a slow manoeuvring struggle: the central squares are held by pieces, and whichever side prepares its pawn break better gets the more active play.

Takes queenside space and the d5 square, which restrains Black's pawns and aims at a slow squeeze. White's bishops work on the long diagonals while the c-pawn does the restraining, and the game stays strategic.

Stakes the centre at once and controls e5, the square Black's thematic break aims for. The bishop on b2 is hemmed in by its own pawn, so White plays on space and the other bishop, in a stable structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Black mirrors White: the bishop takes the long diagonal and aims at the centre, and the king can castle next. A symmetrical, solid answer that keeps all central options open and leads to a patient game of manoeuvring.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 d6.strategy: Builds the set-up in another order: the pawn holds e5 and frees the queen's bishop, and the king's bishop follows next. Black keeps the choice of centre open and gives nothing away, though White speaks first.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 c5.strategy: Takes queenside space and the d4 square before White has a pawn in the centre, a more active course than mirroring. Black plays for a flexible game, but still has to finish the kingside development, and the c-pawn may become a target.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O.strategy: White tucks the king away behind the fianchetto and completes the kingside development before deciding on the central plan. The move commits to a closed, strategic game in which White builds slowly and keeps the choice of pawn structure.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.c4.strategy: Adds the c-pawn: space on the queenside and control of d5 before castling. White drops the plan of a modest centre in favour of restraining Black's central pawns, a slower and more positional game.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn at once, so White plays a queen's-pawn set-up with the bishop behind its structure instead of the slower build-up. White gets space, and Black has to find a way to challenge the pawn.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O.strategy: Black does the same: the king is safe, the position is fully symmetrical, and neither side has yet committed a central pawn. The fight is for who sets the agenda with the next pawn move.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O d6.strategy: Holds e5 and frees the queen's bishop, copying a familiar defensive structure and waiting to see White's plan. Solid and slightly passive, it offers White nothing to attack but concedes the first word in the centre.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O d5.strategy: Claims space at once and makes White's e-pawn advance harder. Black has not yet castled, so the king needs attention soon, and the pawn may become a target of White's pieces and a later c-pawn advance.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..strategy: Supports the squares e4 and c4 with a modest pawn and frees the queen's bishop, building the flexible set-up in which White later plays for a central advance with the e-pawn. Slow, but it keeps the position solid.

Takes queenside space and the d5 square, trading the slow build-up for lasting pressure on the centre from the flank. White's pieces and the c-pawn restrain Black's central pawns, and the game stays strategic, with the e-pawn left at home for now.

Takes the centre with a pawn at once, so White plays a queen's-pawn set-up with the bishop on g2 behind it. White gains space, and Black has to decide how to challenge the pawn, but the quick build-up of the d3 and e4 plan is given up.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..name: King's Indian Attack: Wahls Defence
1.Nf3 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O O-O 5..strategy: Black claims central space at once with a pawn that also controls e4 and c4, denying White's e-pawn its easy advance. In return the structure is committed, and the game stays level and strategic, both sides playing for pawn breaks.

Takes queenside space and the d4 square, a more combative choice that keeps the d-pawn flexible. Black prepares to meet White's e-pawn advance with pressure on the centre, at the price of a c-pawn White can aim at.
A solid set-up in which the pawn holds e5 and frees the queen's bishop. It is safe, but Black has less space than with a pawn on d5 and does little to hinder White's e-pawn advance.
